extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers and authors who are self-editing manuscripts
extracted.subtask_description: A practical checklist and guidance for performing the line-level (word/line/paragraph) edit on fiction manuscripts, after story- and scene-level revisions, to tighten prose and improve readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story Level (developmental edit)
rubrics_metrics.description: The big picture edit: make sure the character arc and the plot are solid; determine if the story is on the correct path and make a plan of action for structural changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach Story Level first (before Scene and Line Level). This is often known as the developmental edit — focus on overall structure, character arcs, and major plot problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene Level
rubrics_metrics.description: Edit each scene to ensure it is doing its job to move the story forward; check that each scene has a specific purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One thing to check at the scene level is Pacing or Scene Balance. Fix scenes that don't advance plot, character, or stakes before doing line edits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Line Level
rubrics_metrics.description: Edit word-by-word, line-by-line, and paragraph-by-paragraph to ensure sentences flow and the story is refined; remove awkward sentences and unnecessary words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the final level of self-editing and the key to reader enjoyment; aim for prose that doesn't trip readers up with tangles and roots.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to Use This Checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat each checklist item as its own editing task; start at the top and move down the list, addressing items separately at first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn how to fix each item, practice improving one item at a time, and later combine items once you can reliably spot them. Use the printable Line Edit Checklist as a quick reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Send cleanest copy to critique partners/beta readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Always send the cleanest copy of your manuscript to readers; it should be line edited first or readers won't see the forest for the trees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critiquers will only point out what isn’t working (and maybe why); it is up to you to revise per their advice. Doing line edits before sharing improves usefulness of feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infodumping / Information dumping
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid information dumping — too much backstory or explaining everything up front signals novice writing and slows the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers prefer a little mystery. Reveal only the necessary pieces of information and withhold what the reader can infer. Give the reader 2 + 2 and let them solve the equation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filtering character experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid filtering the character experience through narrator words that name what a character feels or senses (i.e., 'she felt', 'he saw'), which creates distance instead of intimacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If feedback says 'Show, Don't Tell', you are likely filtering. Study Deep Point of View techniques to minimize filter words and create intimacy. See linked 'Tightened Prose' resources and recommendations (e.g., 'Rivet Your Readers With Deep Point Of View').

rubrics_metrics.name: Crutch words / overused filler words
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and remove crutch words — words and phrases you overuse (often adverbs or filler speech like 'well', 'you know', 'um').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listen to your story read aloud (Google Docs 'Speak' feature or similar) to spot crutch words. Search for common crutch words and compile a checklist to reduce reliance on them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Echo words (repetition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid repeating the same noun or verb over and over (echo words) within a paragraph or page; repetition can distract the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challenge yourself to cut repeats (e.g., reduce 'dog' to once per paragraph). Use synonyms or more specific nouns (Rover, canine, pooch, hound) and a thesaurus to vary language. Tools like Hemingway Editor can help spot repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adverb abuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid overusing adverbs; they often signal weak verb choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace adverb + verb constructions with stronger verbs (e.g., 'walked quietly' → 'tiptoed', 'burn brightly' → 'blazed'). Search for common adverbs and replace them; resources suggested include '1,000 Strong Verbs: For Fiction Writers'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overwritten Prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Cut overwritten passages that tell too much or over-explain — this includes excessive internalization, long-winded monologues, overly detailed setting descriptions, and nano-second action sequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the magic of the story by not explaining the trick. Check character internalization that pulls readers out of action, trim long monologues, and avoid excessive scene-by-scene minutiae.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjective abuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using too many adjectives; excessive adjectives make prose feel juvenile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose stronger, more descriptive nouns instead of piling adjectives on (e.g., 'old car' → 'clunker'; 'tall hair' → 'bouffant'). Use search tools to find and reduce adjective overuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Messy dialogue tags
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer 'said' as the default dialogue tag; avoid overwrought tags that draw attention away from dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use action beats instead of fancy tags when appropriate, but don't overdo it. Messy dialogue tags can ruin otherwise good scenes; study dialogue craft (recommended: 'How to Write Dazzling Dialogue').

rubrics_metrics.name: Vary sentence structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce variety in sentence structure to avoid monotonous rhythm and keep prose engaging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary sentence length, openings, and constructions to create an artful balance on the page; this is an important step toward polished, compelling writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show, Don't Tell
rubrics_metrics.description: Favor showing over telling; let readers experience the character's emotions and sensations rather than being told about them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Closely related to Filtering character experience — eliminate telling language and surface details that distance the reader. See linked 'Tightened Prose' post for fuller checklist of weak words to cut.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passive voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid passive constructions that weaken immediacy and can filter or distance character experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use active voice where possible; passive voice is noted by tools like Hemingway and should be corrected during line edits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use editing tools and read-aloud methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ tools (Hemingway Editor, Text Inspector) and read-aloud features (Google Docs 'Speak') to catch adverbs, passive voice, complicated phrases, readability issues, and overused parts of speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paste text into these apps for analysis (readability score, tagger for parts of speech). Listening to your text read aloud highlights rhythm, crutch words, and awkward phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create visual reminders (print checklist/bookmark)
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep a printed Line Edit Checklist or bookmark near your workspace as a visual cue to apply line-edit habits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Print the free Line Edit Checklist on cardstock and place it near your monitor to keep line-editing priorities top of mind while drafting and revising.
